proof:
# An all-dimensional product bound for two equal captured heights

Let d>=2. A proper oriented section of a d-simplex has exactly two positive affine vertex heights, equal to each other, and all its other vertex heights strictly negative. Let b be the section's barycentric centroid and F the captured volume fraction. If the centroid coordinate of either captured vertex is at most 1/d, then

    F >= d^d product_(j!=r) b_j

for either captured vertex r. In fact the inequality is strict in this stated nondegenerate setting. No bound on the other centroid coordinates is needed. This is a specified-cap comparison, stronger in this scope than the archived central-region minimum-depth theorem. It does not concern mixed-integer fibers.

## 1. Exact cap and section formulas

Scale the two positive heights to one and write the remaining heights as -r_i with r_i>0, i=1,...,d-1. Put

    a_i=1/(1+r_i), t_i=1-a_i, Z=sum_i t_i, L=product_i a_i.

Then

    F=L(1+Z),
    b_0=b_1=(Z^2+sum_i t_i^2)/(2dZ),
    b_(i+1)=a_i(Z+t_i)/(dZ).                           (1)

For a direct derivation, write a uniform barycentric point as independent unit exponentials divided by their sum; the change of variables has Jacobian equal to the sum to power d and proves that representation. The captured event is E_0+E_1>=W, where W=sum_i r_i E_(i+1). The gamma-two survival function is exp(-W)(1+W). Independence gives E[exp(-W)]=L and E[W exp(-W)]=L Z, proving the formula for F.

Let P_j be the derivative of cap probability with respect to vertex height j. Coarea gives P_j=A b_j, where A=sum_j P_j>0 is the coarea section factor. Differentiating the explicit cap formula in a negative height gives

    P_(i+1)=L a_i(Z+t_i).

Symmetry gives P_0=P_1. The cap probability is homogeneous of degree zero in all heights, so Euler's identity gives

    2P_0=sum_i r_i P_(i+1)=L(Z^2+sum_i t_i^2).

Summing these derivatives gives A=d L Z and proves every formula in (1). Differentiation is justified either by the proper interior section and bounded coarea slices, or by the exponentially dominated integral just used. Repeated negative heights cause no denominator singularity.

## 2. A probability-vector product inequality

For any finite nonnegative vector v with sum one, write s=sum v_i^2. Then

    (1+s) product_i(1+v_i) <= 3+s.                     (2)

Here is a self-contained coefficient proof. Let e_j be the elementary symmetric functions of v, with e_0=e_1=1. Their finite sequence is log-concave and has no internal zeros. To see log-concavity without a separate theorem, start with the sequence (1) and successively convolve with (1,v_i). If a is log-concave with contiguous positive support, the new sequence b_j=a_j+t a_(j-1) satisfies

    b_j^2-b_(j-1)b_(j+1)
      =[a_j^2-a_(j-1)a_(j+1)]
       +t[a_j a_(j-1)-a_(j-2)a_(j+1)]
       +t^2[a_(j-1)^2-a_(j-2)a_j]>=0.

The middle bracket is nonnegative by the decreasing consecutive ratios of a; endpoint zeros are harmless. This proves the induction, including v_i=0.

Put e=e_2=(1-s)/2<=1/2. Log-concavity and e_1=1 give e_(j+1)/e_j<=e for j>=2 whenever the denominator is positive. Thus

    sum_(j>=3) e_j <= e^2/(1-e).

Since product(1+v_i)=2+e+sum_(j>=3)e_j and 1+s=2(1-e), this is precisely (2) after expansion. If at least two entries of v are positive, e>0 and the finite tail is strictly smaller than its infinite geometric upper bound, so (2) is strict. If only one is positive, equality holds.

## 3. Product payment

Set v_i=t_i/Z and s=sum_i v_i^2. Substituting (1) and canceling the positive factor L shows that the desired cap product inequality is exactly

    2(1+1/Z) >= (1+s) product_i(1+v_i).               (3)

The captured-coordinate hypothesis in (1) is Z(1+s)<=2, so the left side of (3) is at least 3+s. Equation (2) completes the proof.

For d>=3, all d-1 entries of v are positive and at least two exist, giving strictness in (2). For d=2, v=(1), while 0<Z=t_1<1; thus the first inequality 2(1+1/Z)>=3+s is strict. This proves the stated strictness in every dimension covered.

Zero vertex heights and unequal positive heights are not silently included. The latter case currently has a separate exact algebraic reduction but no proof in this note. Ordinary affine coordinate changes preserve the cap fraction and barycentric centroid; no lattice-preserving normalization is needed or claimed.
